blocks.md: **A cost function for six US airlines over 15 years runs the whole panel toolkit. $F$ tests compare the pooled model with models that add firm effects, year effects or both: firm effects matter enormously, and year effects matter once firms are controlled for. Comparing fixed and random firm effects with a Hausman test does not reject random effects, unlike the wage panel, so here the more efficient estimator is acceptable.**

blocks.title: Source
blocks.md: Section 7 of `Regression_Lecture5.ipynb` (see [Econ 430 L23 Panel Data and Microeconomic Panels](note:econ-430-l23-panel-data-and-microeconomic-panels) for how the notebook maps to lectures). The data are the `USAirlines` panel (Greene): 6 firms, 1970–1984, 90 observations, with cost, output (revenue passenger miles, as an index), fuel price and load factor (average capacity utilisation).

The response is $\ln(COST)$; the inputs are $\ln(OUTPUT)$, its square, $\ln(PRICE)$ and the load factor $LOAD$. Four models differ in their effects ([Fixed Effects Regression](note:fixed-effects-regression)):

| Model | Effects | Residual df | SSE |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pooled | none | 85 | 1.2749 |
| Time | 14 year dummies | 71 | 1.0347 |
| Firm | 5 firm dummies | 80 | 0.2682 |
| Full | year and firm | 66 | 0.1726 |
Each restricted model is tested against the full one with an $F$ test ([F Test of Joint Hypotheses](note:f-test-of-joint-hypotheses)):

| Comparison | Tests | $F$ | $p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Full vs pooled | Year and firm effects jointly (19 restrictions) | 22.19 | $\approx 0$ |
| Full vs time only | Firm effects, given year effects (5) | 65.95 | $\approx 0$ |
| Full vs firm only | Year effects, given firm effects (14) | 2.61 | 0.0046 |
Both sets of effects belong in the model.

blocks.prompt: Compute the $F$ statistic for year effects given firm effects, from $SSE_R = 0.268154$ (firm effects only, 80 residual df) and $SSE_U = 0.172570$ (both, 66 df).

wrong.md: that forgets to divide the numerator by the 14 restrictions
that divides $SSE_U$ by the restricted model's 80 degrees of freedom; the denominator uses the unrestricted model's 66

blocks.md: The notebook repeats the tests with the panel package's "pooled $F$" for each model, which tests that model's effects against no effects at all: year effects alone (without firm controls) give $F(14, 71) = 1.18$, $p = 0.31$, and firm effects alone $F(5, 80) = 60.07$. Year effects look unimportant until firm differences are removed, because the large firm differences swamp the common year pattern.

blocks.prompt: Year effects are insignificant on their own ($F = 1.18$, $p = 0.31$) but significant once firm effects are included ($F = 2.61$, $p = 0.005$). Why?

options.md: The second test has more observations
Without firm effects, the large permanent cost differences between airlines stay in the error, inflating it and hiding the smaller common year pattern
Firm and year dummies are perfectly collinear
options.feedback: If they were, the full model could not be estimated.

options.md: Year effects are only identified with firm effects
options.feedback: They are identified either way; what changes is the noise they are judged against.

blocks.why: The $F$ statistic scales by the residual variance. Removing firm differences cuts the residual sum of squares from 1.03 (time-only model) to 0.17 (full model), so the same year pattern stands out.

blocks.md: The estimates with both effects show year effects rising steadily from 0.055 in 1971 to about 0.73 by 1981–1984, relative to 1970: costs rose about 73 log points over the period for reasons common to all airlines, beyond output, fuel prices and load. The firm effects, relative to firm 1, range from $-0.24$ (firm 3) to $+0.11$ (firm 4), most with intervals that include zero.

blocks.md: Across models the coefficient on fuel price is unstable: 0.40 with firm effects only, 0.13 (insignificant) with both effects, $-0.46$ with year effects only. Fuel prices move mostly over time and are common to all airlines, so year dummies absorb most of their variation.
With firm effects only, fixed and random effects estimates are close:

blocks.md: The Hausman test ([Hausman Test](note:hausman-test)) gives $\chi^2_{(4)} = 5.62$, $p = 0.23$: random effects is not rejected and, being more efficient, is used ([Random Effects Model](note:random-effects-model)).

blocks.prompt: For the airlines, Hausman $\chi^2_{(4)} = 5.62$ with $p = 0.23$. What should you conclude?

options.md: No evidence that the firm effects are correlated with the regressors; random effects is consistent and more efficient here

options.feedback: A large $p$-value means *not* rejecting $H_0$, which favours random effects.
The Hausman test compares two estimators; the $F$ test already showed the firm effects are large.

options.md: The test is invalid because there are only four coefficients
options.feedback: The degrees of freedom simply equal the number of compared coefficients.

blocks.why: The two estimators differ by little relative to their sampling variability, as $H_0$ predicts. A caution: with only six firms, the variance of the random firm effect is estimated from six draws, so "random effects" rests on thin evidence about the population of firms.

blocks.title: Correction to the lecture notebook
blocks.md: The cell that plots the firm effects is commented "Visualizing year effects". The comments on the panel-package tests ("Case 2: only time effects (not controlled for firm)") describe tests of each kind of effect *without* the other, which is why they differ from the ANOVA comparisons above, which control for the other effect.

sections.heading: What to be able to do

blocks.md:
1. Set up pooled, time, firm and two-way fixed effects models and test each kind of effect with an $F$ test.
2. Explain why a test of one kind of effect depends on whether the other is controlled for, and read year and firm effect plots.
3. Choose between fixed and random firm effects with a Hausman test.
